transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Hi. Um, I guess what finally pushed me to come in is this thing where I just… I keep getting up when I’m supposed to stay seated. Like during sprint planning at work, which is already kind of structured and everyone’s on the call, I’ll suddenly feel like I need water, or I’ll remember something in the other room and just get up before I’ve really thought it through.

And it’s not only work. It happens on mortgage calls too, which feels especially ridiculous because those are important and I know I should be sitting there, listening carefully, being an adult about it. But then I’m up checking something, or wandering to get a glass, and part of me is aware that I’m doing it and thinking, “Why can’t you just stay put for half an hour?” It’s not dramatic exactly, but it’s happening enough that it’s bothering me.
Do you often act on sudden impulses without thinking through the consequences, even when you know it might not be the best idea?

Yeah, I think so, though the main way it shows up is probably this getting-up thing. Like, I’ll be in sprint planning at work, and I know I’m supposed to just stay seated and pay attention because people are talking through priorities and tickets and all of that, but then I’ll suddenly think, “Oh, I need water,” or “Wait, I should check that thing in the other room,” and I’m already standing before I’ve really decided whether that’s a good idea.

Same with mortgage calls, which makes me feel kind of embarrassed because those are important, and I do know there can be consequences if I miss something or seem like I’m not fully present. But in the moment it’s like the impulse to move wins before the more sensible part of my brain catches up. Then a minute later I’m thinking, “Why did I just do that? Why couldn’t I just sit still for this call?” So… yes, not in some huge reckless way, but I do act before thinking in that specific way, and it’s been happening enough that it’s one of the reasons I came in.
Did you notice similar difficulties with staying seated or acting on impulse when you were a child, or is this something that’s mostly started more recently?

Yeah… I think it was there when I was a kid too. I mean, I don’t remember every detail clearly, but I do remember in elementary school teachers moving my desk sometimes, or putting me closer to them, because I’d keep popping up or turning around or talking when I wasn’t supposed to.

And I remember getting reminded to stay seated a lot. Not in a “bad kid” way exactly — I usually understood the work and could do it — but I’d rush through things or blurt out answers before I was called on. I can picture that feeling of knowing the answer and just saying it, like my hand or my mouth got ahead of me. So I guess it doesn’t feel brand new. The adult version is more like getting up during meetings or calls, but the basic thing of moving or acting before I pause… that does feel familiar from childhood.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of acting on impulse (e.g., getting up during important meetings without thinking it through) and a history of similar behavior in childhood (e.g., blurting out answers, being unable to stay seated) point strongly toward a lifelong pattern consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation. This pattern rules out most mood disorders (e.g., F32, F33), anxiety-related disorders (F06.3, F06.7), and other organic or personality-related conditions (F07.0, F07.8, F07.9). F90.0 (Hyperkinetic disorder of childhood, which maps closely to ADHD) is the most accurate code based on the information so far, and further questioning is unlikely to change this trajectory.
